hero.lede: The Memorial is not a political vehicle. It is our national shrine, the grave of 103,000 names. Now they want to fill it with activism and contested history. Our fallen cannot object.

happened.heading: A decision no Australian was asked about
body: In August 2022, behind closed doors, the Council of the Australian War Memorial decided to build a gallery inside the Memorial devoted to anti-colonial activism, and contested history.

There was no Act of Parliament. There was no public consultation. There was no legal advice. Asked at Senate Estimates whether the Council would even check that it had the power, the Memorial's Director said there were no plans to.

The decision was recorded in a single paragraph of a council minute. Those minutes did not surface for nine months, and only then because a Senator asked for them. When a member of the public later asked for the policy under Freedom of Information, the Memorial replied that no documents existed. On review, it reversed and confirmed the policy does exist.
The gallery is now confirmed. Roughly 200 square metres, the size of a singles tennis court, on the main concourse at the entrance. The Director calls it "the next step."

responsible.heading: Kim Beazley knows better than this
body: Kim Beazley has been Minister for Defence. He has been Australia's Ambassador to the United States. He has been Governor of Western Australia. He is the son of a man this country respected. There is no one in public life who better understands what the Memorial is for, and what it costs a nation to fill it.

He is the decision's loudest public advocate. On national radio he dismissed the Memorial's telling of our history as a fiction, and he has promised to use the Memorial itself to make Australians accept his version of the story. His words are on the record, at the bottom of this page.
responsible.emBody: That is a man describing the nation's shrine as his to instruct us with.
responsible.close: Kim Beazley can be remembered as a Defence Minister and Governor. Or he can be remembered as the man who attempted to introduce activism into Australia's history. He cannot get away with it.
responsible.cta: Tell him no. Sign the petition.

items.title: It is sacred, not a museum.
items.body: The Memorial is sacred ground. It bears the names of 103,000 Australians who died serving this country, and it is where their families come to mourn. Introducing activism into that space is not something a nation does lightly. This history already has a home: the National Museum of Australia, the Australian Museum, and the $316.5 million Ngurra precinct. It is not this one.

items.title: It was done by stealth.
items.body: No Act. No consultation. No legal advice. A single paragraph in a minute, nine months to release, and an FOI answer that said no documents existed until it was challenged. Whatever you think of our history, our national memorial should not change in secret.

items.title: It redefined what Australia is.
items.body: The controversial historians behind this have been explicit. One has proposed placing a second tomb beside the Tomb of the Unknown Australian Soldier, so that "those who fought for empire would be at rest with those who fought against the empire." The campaign's own website calls for names added to the Roll of Honour. The same historian co-wrote a book asking whether it is "not now time for Australia to cast aside" the Anzac legend. This is not an addition to Anzac. It is a replacement for it.

items.title: It is costing $550 million.
items.body: The Memorial's redevelopment has been funded at $548.7 million. Three in four Australians say that money would be better spent on health, education and veterans' services. Fewer than one in five support putting frontier conflict in the Memorial at all. It is being built anyway, with money that is not the Council's, for a purpose Parliament never authorised.

notSaying.heading: Where it belongs, and who decides
body: This is not an argument about whether the history is true. It is an argument about where it belongs, and about who gets to decide.

In 2018 the Memorial's own Director wrote that the story "should be told at the National Museum of Australia, not the Australian War Memorial." That is our position. It was the Memorial's position too, until the Council changed its mind without changing the law.

petition.heading: To Kim Beazley, Chair of the Council of the Australian War Memorial
letter: The Australian War Memorial does not belong to its Council. It belongs to every Australian family that lost someone, and it is governed by an Act of Parliament that says what it is for: war and warlike operations by the Defence Force.

Your Council has decided to put the colonial frontier conflicts inside that building. You did it without an Act of Parliament, without consulting a single Australian, and without taking legal advice on whether you had the power at all.
You do not have that power. Only Parliament does.

You of all people know what that building is. You have been Minister for Defence. You have represented this country in Washington. You know that the Memorial is a shrine and not a lecture theatre, and that the names on those walls were put there by families, not by curators.
We call on the Australian Government, Kim Beazley and the Australian War Memorial board to maintain the sanctity of our Australian War Memorial by:

from further historical revisions without approval from the Parliament of Australia.

letterClose: We do not deny what happened on the frontier. We say it belongs where the Memorial's own Director said it belonged in 2018: at the National Museum of Australia.
This is not yours to change.

sidebar.heading: Why this petition is addressed to one man
body: Kim Beazley chairs the Council that made this decision and he has become its loudest public advocate. He has said the Memorial told Australians "a fiction." He has said the frontier belongs there "because it is by that means we established ourselves." He has said he will "make sure the War Memorial makes all of us understand."
He can stop this. That is why the petition is his.

variations.subject: The War Memorial is not the Council's to change
variations.body:
Dear Minister,

I am writing about the decision of the Council of the Australian War Memorial to place colonial frontier conflict displays inside the Memorial.

The Memorial is governed by an Act of Parliament that covers war and warlike operations by the Defence Force. The Council made this change without an Act of Parliament, without public consultation, and without taking legal advice on whether it had the power at all.

I ask you to maintain the sanctity of the Australian War Memorial by:

1. Halting and removing the frontier conflicts and other contested history that contravene the War Memorial's governing Act.
2. Abstaining from further historical revisions without approval from the Parliament of Australia.

I would appreciate a response setting out your position.

Yours sincerely,

donate.heading: Australians do not even know this is happening
body: That is not an accident. It was done quietly, and quiet is how it stays unless someone pays to break the silence.
We do not have a member of parliament. We do not have a broadcaster. We have a list of names and whatever we can put behind it.

Every dollar goes to reaching Australians who do not yet know that the Australian War Memorial is being changed into something else, and to making sure Kim Beazley cannot pretend the country is behind him.

about.heading: Who we are
about.lede: We are Australians who think the Australian War Memorial should remain what Parliament built it to be.
who: Among us are veterans, the children and grandchildren of the fallen, historians and ordinary people who have stood at that wall and found a name. We are not a political party and we are not funded by one.
We came together because a decision was made about the most significant building in this country by fourteen people nobody elected, and because nobody asked.

believe.title: A shrine
believe.body: The Memorial is a shrine. Shrines are for grief, not for argument.

believe.title: History has a home
believe.body: Frontier violence happened and should be taught. The National Museum of Australia, the Australian Museum and the $316.5 million Ngurra precinct exist to do exactly that.

believe.title: Parliament decides
believe.body: An Act of Parliament means what it says until Parliament changes it. Not until a Council decides it would prefer otherwise.

evidence.heading: The evidence, with sources
evidence.lede: Everything on this page is sourced. We have published the citations because we expect to be checked, and because the people on the other side of this argument have not been.

sections.heading: The Act does not cover it
body: The Australian War Memorial Act 1980 defines active service as "active service in war or in warlike operations by members of the Defence Force." The words frontier, Aboriginal, Indigenous and 1788 appear nowhere in it. Parliament has amended the Act eighteen times since 1981 and has never extended it to the frontier. No bill to do so has ever been introduced.
The people campaigning for the change have themselves proposed amending the Act to allow it, which is an admission that as written it does not.

sections.heading: The Memorial used to say so itself
body: The Memorial published that it "is not the appropriate institution" and pointed to the National Museum. A 2014 article on its own website said the Act's definition "does not include the internal conflict between Indigenous populations and colonial powers of the day." At Senate Estimates in November 2022, the Director confirmed that was still the Memorial's formal position.

In 2018 the Director wrote: "This story and the story of Indigenous opposition to European settlement and expansion should be told. However, this Australian History should be told at the National Museum of Australia, not the Australian War Memorial."
Nothing in the Act has changed since. Only the Council has.

sections.heading: No legal advice was taken
body: Asked at Senate Estimates whether the Council would seek advice: "There are no plans to take legal advice simply because we believe we have the discretion available to us to be able to do this."

sections.heading: The paper trail
body: Decided at Council Meeting No. 178, 19 August 2022, in a single paragraph. Minutes released nine months later after a Senator asked. Published twelve months later. An FOI applicant told in April 2025 that no documents existed, then told in June 2025 that the policy exists after all.

sections.heading: The scale
body: $548.7 million redevelopment. Roughly 200 square metres devoted to the frontier, at the entrance, on the main concourse. The Director calls it "the next step."

sections.heading: Where the public is
body: A UNSW survey of 1,500 Australians found 16 per cent support including frontier conflicts at the Memorial. Ten per cent had heard of the frontier wars at all.
